✅ Approved the contribution.
Comment: This puzzle's statement is straightforward, it includes an example for each operation so you don't need to look up truth tables, and it's possible to solve it quickly, especially if you're familiar with bit-wise operations.

✅ Approved the contribution.
Comment: Good difficulty and time for a clash

Good puzzle. Gave me a means and reason to learn about python's bitwise operators; although, I did it without them for the sake of it.

Forgive the pointless comment, I'm doing the quest map.

Goal
* Consider explaining each bitwise operation used in the contribution, e.g.

Assume [[x]] and [[y]] are bits:
• [[x]] {{AND}} [[y]] = 1 if [[x]] = [[y]] = 1; otherwise 0
• [[x]] {{OR}} [[y]] = 1 if [[x]] = 1 or [[y]] = 1; otherwise 0
• (and similarly for the other operators)

Input
* Please add "separated by a space" at the end.

Game modes
* Consider disabling Reverse mode. In that mode, players don't have access to the statement and may need to look up definitions online in order to complete the task.

Cases
* Please revise the cases so that:
  (a) the lengths of the binary numbers are similar between each test and its corresponding validator, and
  (b) different input lengths are covered in a balanced manner.
  
  Specifically:

  • NOR (test and validator): use binary numbers of around 13 to 18 digits

  • AND (validator): use binary numbers of around 20 digits

  • XNOR (test and validator): use binary numbers of around 25 to 30 digits

* Binary numbers with leading zeros are not adequately covered at the moment. Please make sure both tests and validators cover this situation, and [[a]] having leading zeros and [[b]] having leading zeros are equally covered.

* Additionally, please ensure that for every operator, all binary digit combinations appear in *both* the tests and validators, i.e. 0 op 0, 0 op 1, 1 op 0 and 1 op 1. Revise any existing cases where a combination is missing.

Thanks.

Thanks for the feedback!

I've applied all of your advices.

I'm a bit disappointed for the Reverse mode, since it is my favourite style of play, but I understand your reasons.

I've updated the constraints so that the maximum number for A and B is 2^25-1, and made each test case 4 digits longer than the previous one to cover all the range.

I've also tried to explain what is a bitwise operation in the Goal, but I'm unsure if it is clear enough.

Feel free to add remarks if you think it is needed!
Thanks anyway for the funny comment!
A lot of thanks for the kind comment :)

No problem!

I understand your disappointment regarding my suggestion to disable Reverse mode. If the task involved AND, OR and XOR only, I think Reverse mode would still be reasonable. However, since NAND, NOR and XNOR are also required, it may become a bit too difficult in Reverse mode when the operator definitions are hidden from the players.

Covering binary string lengths in the test cases in a progressive way is systematic and clear. I like your new approach.

Goal
* XOR: Please change "!=" to "≠".

* I think the explanatory paragraphs could be simplified. Right now, the detailed walkthrough of comparing the lowest bit, then the second-lowest bit, and so on makes the section fairly long for a simple puzzle, and may unintentionally suggest that a manual bit-by-bit method is the only way to go.

I'd suggest replacing "A bitwise operation is… expected return values:" (i.e. the second sentence up to the sentence before the operator definitions) with:

********************
A bitwise operation applies a logical operation to each pair of corresponding bits in two binary numbers.

Built-in bitwise operators available in your language may be used. Alternatively, you may implement the operations using the definitions below.

Assume [[x]] and [[y]] are bits. The required operators are:
********************

Constraints / Cases
* Final constraint: I'd like to propose changing "[[a]] and [[b]]" to "Either [[a]] or [[b]]", since leading zeros should only be added to make the lengths of [[a]] and [[b]] match.

* If you agree with the previous point, please also revise NAND (test and validator) so that only [[b]] starts with two leading zeros while [[a]] has none.

Cases
* XNOR (test): Please swap [[a]] and [[b]] so that [[a]] starts with 3 leading zeros.

* XNOR (validator): Please revise [[a]] so that it contains 3 or more leading zeros.

Thanks.

Thank you for the reply!
I've applied everything, once again.

I too was uncomfortable about having both the numbers contain leading zeros. That was overly complex for no real added value, so it is gone now. :)

Many thanks for the enlightened remarks, especially regarding Reverse mode!
